Le ring contre la rue : à Saint-Michel,: The Ring Versus the Street: In Saint-Michel, Boxing Steers Youth Away from Delinquency
À Saint-Michel, un programme local utili: In Saint-Michel, a local program uses boxing to support young people exposed to delinquency and offer them lasting prospects.
Keoma Ali Al-Ahmadieh s'entraîne avec le: Keoma Ali Al-Ahmadieh trains with coach El Mostafa Lyousfi. Photo credit: Nouri Nesrouche
Il y a quelques semaines, en travaillant: A few weeks ago, while working on another article, I came across a rather unusual initiative aimed at pulling teenagers off the street and channelling their energy, while offering them new prospects.
Cet article est le fruit de plusieurs vi: This article is the result of several visits to The Corner boxing club, a partner in the program, as well as interviews conducted on site with young participants, coaches and staff from the Loisirs Communautaires Saint-Michel (LCSM) community centre.
Les jeunes rencontrés ont accepté de tém: The young people I met agreed to speak of their own free will. Some, whose identities we have chosen to keep anonymous, agreed to share episodes of their lives they are not proud of and mentioned aspects of their legal history without going into the nature of it. Their words have been reported faithfully, with respect for what they said and for their privacy.
L’objectif de cet article est de documen: The aim of this article is to document a local prevention and support initiative, in the spirit of solutions journalism, without claiming to offer an exhaustive evaluation or to generalize the results observed.
<strong>Avant même d’entrer dans le gym,: Even before you step into the gym, you can hear shouts echoing in the stairwell. Then, at the top of the stairs, the dull thud of punches against heavy bags and the rhythm of drills take over. It’s 6 p.m. at the corner of Bélanger Street and Saint-Michel Boulevard, and about thirty young people are training at The Corner boxing club. Many of them are part of a special program.
<strong>Depuis l’été 2025, ce gym est en: Since the summer of 2025, this gym has in fact become one of the anchor points of a program set up by the Loisirs Communautaires de Saint-Michel (LCSM) community centre in partnership with professional boxer Abed El-Safadi. The goal? To offer an alternative to local youth exposed to delinquency, building on a very real interest in boxing.
« On avait beaucoup de bagarres de rue »: “We had a lot of street fights,” says Ismaël Benyettou, a psychosocial worker and the project lead at <l1>LCSM</l1>. In the summer of 2025, several young people in the neighbourhood were staging improvised boxing matches with no supervision. “For them, it was just play. But you don’t know how strong the other person is. It can get out of hand,” he explains between greeting newcomers, as the young people trickle into the gym, alone or in small groups.
Le phénomène inquiète le voisinage et me: The phenomenon worried people in the area and highlighted a void after school hours. “After school, we were ending up with kids who could potentially get hurt,” he continues. Looking at the situation, the LCSM team identified a possible lever: these teenagers’ strong interest in boxing.
Plutôt que d’essayer d’interdire les com: Rather than trying to ban the fights, the centre decided to structure them. Partners in the neighbourhood were approached. Among them, <l1>Abed El-Safadi,</l1> who already takes part in some LCSM activities to promote boxing, agreed to get involved. That is how the project Réfléchir autrement par la culture et le sport was born.
<strong>Un partenariat de terrain sans r: A grassroots partnership with no miracle recipe
Le programme s’adresse à des jeunes de 1: The program is for young people aged 12 to 21. Boxing is its athletic pillar, complemented by a cultural component focused on music through LCSM’s La Station studio. “Our idea is to go with their interests, but also to offer them something else,” explains Ismaël Benyettou.
Séance d'entrainement au club The Corner: Training session at The Corner. Photo credit: Nouri Nesrouche
Quinze jeunes sont déjà inscrits, mais l: Fifteen young people are already registered, but as luck would have it, during our visit that evening, six new participants were signed up by Ismaël, whom we met on site. “It moves fast thanks to word of mouth,” he observes. Young people who aren’t registered end up wanting to join their friends, he explains. They are drawn as much by boxing as by the group’s atmosphere.
L’encadrement fait l’objet d’un équilibr: The supervision is a delicate balancing act. Certain behaviours would not be tolerated in a strictly athletic setting. “We once had an incident with some young people Abed caught smoking cannabis downstairs outside the building,” Ismaël Benyettou says. “If they had just been regular gym members, we would have told them not to come back. But here, we work together to keep them and get them re-engaged.”
<strong>Abed El-Safadi : transmettre san: Abed El-Safadi: passing on knowledge without playing the saviour
Âgé de 28 ans, Abed El-Safadi est né à M: Aged 28, Abed El-Safadi was born in Montréal to Palestinian-Moroccan parents. A former professional boxer, he fought six pro bouts between 2018 and 2023. Injuries and the pandemic slowed his career, but did not break his bond with the ring.
Abed El-Safadi (à gauche) défie François: Abed El-Safadi (left) squares off against François Beaudoin. Photo credit: Nouri Nessrouche
Pendant sa convalescence, il ouvre le cl: During his recovery, he opened The Corner boxing club with his partner, El Mostafa Lyousfi. “It was our turn to give back to the community,” he says. When LCSM contacted him, the idea made immediate sense. “My partner and I had been thinking for a while about a way to help young people. It came at just the right time when Ismaël made us the proposal and brought in the kids from the neighbourhood.”
Le gym accueille à la fois des boxeurs d: The gym welcomes both competitive boxers and teenagers simply looking for an after-school activity. Young people registered through LCSM get heavily reduced rates, which also cover equipment. “The goal isn’t to make a profit, it’s for them to come and train,” Abed insists. The formula is clearly bearing fruit, as the registered youth are taking to the training. “They feel like they’re in the best possible gym,” notes Ismaël Benyettou. “It motivates them to stay.”
<strong>« Ici, au moins, il y a un intér: “Here, at least, there’s a reason to be here”
Zakary Zouki, 19 ans, est arrivé au gym: Zakary Zouki, 19, came to The Corner by another route. Before boxing, he experienced the joy of learning and playing music through LCSM’s offerings. “I discovered the La Station studio because a friend brought me there. It got me out of my everyday routine,” he says. He recalls that at the time, he was going in circles with no clear goal. “I was doing the same things, I didn’t really have a purpose in life.”
Pour lui, le programme de boxe s’inscrit: For him, the boxing program is a continuation. Not a dramatic break, but an extension. “I need to improve physically, to fill my time. Here, it’s exercise, conditioning. A healthy body in a healthy mind.” He says little about his past difficulties, which he prefers to keep to himself. But he stresses the relationship of trust with the team at the Saint-Michel community centre. “They were there for me in some very hard times. They’re real people.”
Pour Rami, étudiant en administration de: For Rami, a business administration student at CEGEP, boxing arrived at a turning point. At 16, he had run-ins with the law over car thefts. He could then have sunk deeper into delinquency, a one-way trip. But when he was at a dead end, he was lucky enough to be offered a helping hand. “We sat down with Ismaël, he helped me find solutions,” he says. Three years later, he says he’s “clean.”
Depuis qu’il a intégré le programme en n: Since joining the program in November, Rami has trained four or five times a week. “Either I’m here, or I’m at home doing nothing, or I’m outside doing pointless stuff,” he continues. “Here, at least, there’s a reason to be here.” He also mentions his surprise when he arrived: “We were paying a lot less, so we figured we’d be treated differently. But no. Everyone welcomed us.”
Like Rami, René is from Saint-Michel. He is currently finishing community service hours imposed as part of probation. He prefers not to go into detail. “I pleaded guilty to something,” he says simply. Since November, he has been at the gym almost every day. “Boxing calms me down. It puts me in harmony with society,” he confides, running his fingers through his hair, which is pulled back in a ponytail.
Ses mots sont parfois hésitants, mais le: His words are sometimes hesitant, but the change is clear: “Before, I didn’t really pay attention to myself. Now, I focus more on myself, on my lifestyle.” Even once he has finished his community service hours, he plans to keep coming. “The people here are good people. You get attached fast.”
Pour François Beaudoin, directeur généra: For François Beaudoin, executive director of LCSM, the project is part of a broader transformation of the organization. Present in the neighbourhood for more than 25 years, the centre recently rethought its mission around three areas: seniors, families and youth.
« Saint-Michel, j’y suis depuis l’âge de: “I’ve been in Saint-Michel since I was six. I’ve seen the good sides, the not-so-good, the worst,” he says. In the face of violence, dropping out and marginalization, the goal is not to multiply one-off activities but to ensure follow-up, explains the director, who came by this evening to make sure things were running smoothly. “After three months, we don’t cut them loose and let them become statistics,” he says.
Le volet boxe a d’abord suscité des réti: The boxing component initially met with reluctance. “People told us, ‘You’re pulling them out of violence to put them back into violence.’ That’s false. Boxing channels frustration in a safe place,” says Mr. Beaudoin, who already sees results backing up his choice. The program also draws on professional resources: psychoeducators, sports psychology specialists, institutional partnerships.
L’idée, à terme, est de responsabiliser: The idea, eventually, is to give the young people responsibility, even to bring them on as community outreach workers: “They know the street. With proper support, they can serve the community.”
Dans la salle, les entraînements se pour: In the room, training continues. In the ring, Keoma Ali Al-Ahmadieh, ranked eighth in the world in the 60 kg division, works under the watchful eye of his coach, El Mostafa Lyousfi. A few metres away, teenagers from the neighbourhood repeat the same movements, corrected by former champions. That evening, <l1>Rénald Boisvert</l1>, a well-known figure in Montréal boxing, is also moving among them. In this Saint-Michel gym, unknown young people rub shoulders with local ring legends. Under the roof hangs that familiar boxing-gym smell, a mix of sweat and leather, and a friendly, easygoing atmosphere.
À l’entrée, un écran géant diffuse la de: At the entrance, a giant screen is showing the semifinal of the Africa Cup of Nations. Morocco is on the pitch. Between drills, some stop and look up. At every dangerous play, shouts erupt. Then, at the final whistle, the Moroccan victory sets off an explosion of joy. Gloves drop for a moment. Training resumes. The evening goes on.
